subject: Computer Networking
title: Dyn DNS Attack (2016)
description: A micro-lesson that makes Dyn DNS Attack (2016) usable.

hook.text: On October 21, 2016, Twitter, Netflix, Reddit, and Spotify all went down. The internet's phone book was attacked.

buildup.text: The Mirai botnet launched a massive DDoS against Dyn, a major DNS provider used by thousands of sites.

discovery.text: Mirai had hijacked hundreds of thousands of IoT devices — cameras, DVRs, routers — all with default passwords.

twist.text: When Dyn couldn't respond, browsers couldn't find those sites — even though the servers themselves were fine.

climax.text: The attack came in three waves over a full day. One of the largest DDoS events ever recorded.

punchline.text: Unsecured cameras took down Twitter. IoT security matters.

quiz.question: What devices did the Mirai botnet use to attack Dyn?
options: IoT devices like cameras and routers with default passwords
Personal laptops infected with email viruses

details.summary: In October 2016, the Mirai botnet launched a massive DDoS attack against Dyn, a major DNS provider. The attack used hundreds of thousands of compromised IoT devices and took down DNS resolution for Twitter, Netflix, Reddit, GitHub, and many other major sites across the eastern United States.
details.whyItMatters: The Dyn attack demonstrated that insecure IoT devices could be weaponized to take down critical internet infrastructure. It made IoT security a mainstream concern.
takeaways: The Mirai botnet used compromised IoT devices as attack weapons
Attacking DNS infrastructure can take down hundreds of sites
The incident highlighted IoT default password vulnerabilities

faq.question: How did the Mirai botnet work?
faq.answer: Mirai scanned the internet for IoT devices using default usernames and passwords like admin/admin. It infected cameras, routers, and DVRs, then coordinated them to flood targets with traffic. At peak, the botnet controlled over 600,000 devices.

faq.question: Why was attacking a DNS provider so effective?
faq.answer: DNS translates domain names to IP addresses. When Dyn could not respond to DNS queries, browsers could not find the IP addresses for major websites. The sites were technically running but unreachable. Attacking DNS is like destroying the phone book.
